Can we really know
what color a dinosaur was?
For a long time,
the colors in paleoart
were pure guesswork.
Then, in 2010,
researchers looked at fossil
feathers under powerful
electron microscopes and
found something that changed
everything.
It started in northeastern
China.
In 1996, a farmer
in Liaoning Province found
Sinosauropteryx, a small
predatory dinosaur with
a fringe of simple,
hair-like filaments along
its back and tail.
It was the first
non-bird dinosaur found
with feather-like coverings.
The scaly, lizard-like
raptors of nineties films
soon looked outdated.
In 2007, scientists found
quill knobs on the
forearm bone of a
Velociraptor.
In living birds,
these small bumps anchor
large wing feathers.
So Velociraptor almost
certainly had feathered arms.
It was not a
scaly monster, but a
feathered, bird-like hunter
about the size of a turkey.
In 2010, the researchers
found tiny structures called
melanosomes, which hold
pigment.
Different shapes of
melanosomes give different
colors in living birds.
By comparing them,
scientists could start
to estimate the real
colors of extinct animals.
Sinosauropteryx was one
of the first dinosaurs
to get a color.
The 2010 study found
that its tail had
alternating bands,
reddish-brown and pale,
a striped tail a
little like a red panda's.
A later study,
in 2017, suggested it
was darker on top
and lighter underneath,
with a dark band
across the eyes,
like a bandit mask.
Soon other dinosaurs followed.
Anchiornis, a small
feathered dinosaur from
China, was found to
have a mostly gray
and black body,
white wing feathers with
black tips, and a
reddish crown of feathers
on its head.
And in 2012,
a study of Microraptor
found that its black
feathers probably had a
glossy, iridescent sheen,
like a modern crow
or starling.
After these discoveries,
some artists put feathers
on almost every dinosaur,
and giant tyrannosaurs
began to look like
huge, fluffy birds.
But in 2017,
a study of skin
impressions from
Tyrannosaurus and its
relatives found small scales
on the neck,
hips and tail.
So adult Tyrannosaurus
was probably mostly scaly.
Within a few years,
dinosaurs went from pure
guesswork to animals with
colors backed by evidence.
The full story of
how pictures of extinct
animals changed is on
Miya's Lab.
